101.t: Basie as king of space and time; Neal Hefti's tempo
101.s: Terry says Basie taught space and time, shown when he fixed Hefti's tempo for 'L'il Darlin''.
101.q: Ever since then, every time we played [scats], Sweets would stand up and take his big solo. But I’ll tell you about this cat, Basie, he, although Ellington was more endowed with harmony and theory and so forth, Basie was the king of mother wit as far as tempo, and he taught us all the greatest…

101.t: Playing with Basie's rhythm section and his use of space
101.s: Freddie Green, Walter Page and Jo Jones as a well-oiled machine and Basie's economical comping.
101.q: No. Walter Page had long since been out of the band when I – of course I did work in the band for a while with Papa Jo, and of course on many other occasions I worked with Jo: studios – jazz studio gigs and record sessions and so forth. But I never worked with Big Walter Page.

1.t: How King Oliver's rhythm section shaped Basie's
1.s: Barker says the banjo gave way to a subtle bounce in rhythm guitar, which Bennie Moten and Count Basie took from King Oliver's band.
1.ch: Professional start and leaving New Orleans
1.q: You got that from that, that rhythm section. Bennie Moten got that [expletive deleted] from King Oliver’s band. If you hear some of the King Oliver records, Canal Street Blues with Armstrong and Oliver, and you listen to Count Basie’s band, you’ll hear the same thing there which was done ten years…

1.t: Benny Carter's rhythm section with Heywood, Spencer and Johnny Williams
1.s: Danny recalls his rhythm section in Carter's band and Benny's approval giving prestige before battles of bands.
1.ch: Danny's rise through New York bands to Cab Calloway
1.q: Well, who's in the rhythm section? Danny Barker, Johnny Williams, O'Neil Spencer, and who else... Who was on piano...? Eddie Heywood on piano.

676.t: Rhythm sections, Shorty's band, Nat Pierce and Diva
676.s: Basie-fan rhythm section in Shorty Sherock's wartime band, how Nat Pierce joined, and the all-girl Diva band.
676.q: You know that rhythm section really characterized different bands. If they played that style, that was their ideal. And when Shorty Sherock got his big band and got a date at Glen Island Casino, his rhythm section were Basie fans. As a matter of fact, Nat Pierce, you may have heard of him, he was a…

604.t: How Basie led from the keyboard
604.s: Everything emanated from Basie at the piano, with Freddie Green; he had cues for soloists, the audience and pretty girls.
604.q: And I never realized how everything we played emanated from Bill at the keyboard. And if you isolate everything else and listen to the way he engineered every chart, every arrangement, there was certain ways to play chords and cues and figures. It was just marvelous the way he did it. He knew how…

838.t: Basie rhythm section and Freddie Green
838.s: Eddie Jones, Basie, Sonny Payne and Freddie Green; Green's easygoing temperament.
838.q: He was a very easy going type of person. Very level. Of course he could, if he did get upset it was kind of fun to see.

215.t: Why the Basie rhythm section and Freddie Green were unmatched
215.s: Bucky explains Freddie Green's four-four chunking and why the rhythm section never played the band's figures.
215.q: Well you know when you have four rhythm, and you know what you’re doing, the guitar is the last guy to be hired and the first guy to be fired. But in Freddie Green’s case, without Freddie there’s no band. Because he gave that rhythm section — and Count Basie played sparingly, never overplayed, he…

549.t: What makes the Basie band distinctive
549.s: He describes the rhythmic revolution of the 1930s and how the Basie band embodied it as an ensemble; his mentors' deaths.
549.ch: Basie alumni and childhood in Hollis
549.q: Well that it’s an orchestra that is able to incorporate, without everyone being a genius, the rhythmic revolution of the 1930s. But I don’t think I could have told you that in 1956. I mean in other words the suppleness of the beat that is elasticising and making more fluid the energy of swinging…

68.s: Basie loved tenors, starting with Herschel and Lester, and had Walter Page, Jo Jones and Freddie Green.
68.q: Yeah he loved tenors. You see in those days, you only had one tenor player, featured tenor player, but he always had two so he started out with Herschel and Lester. So he had two of the world’s greatest and wasn’t nobody — he had to make it. So when they went to New York they just chopped everybody…

365.t: Helen Humes, the Basie rhythm section and piano-led bands
365.s: He praises the tight Basie rhythm section and says a pianist leader keeps a rhythm section together.
365.q: Yeah. She was with Basie. Now she could have told you some things about Basie and the band. You would have loved to talk to her. Too bad she’s gone.

226.t: Reputation as part of the Jimmy Jones–Denzil Best rhythm section
226.s: Their rhythm section was hired as a unit; Levy says he was no great soloist but was reliable and had plenty of work.
226.q: I think I was – I think most of the things we did was because of the rhythm section, the style of the rhythm section together. We got hired a lot of times for that, for the rhythm section, for being together, and what we played together and the reputation we had established in over a year working…

137.t: The Kansas City rhythm section with Buster Smith
137.s: For the Kansas City concert Durham played guitar with Smith on piano, Gene Ramey and Joe Jones, which he says amazed listeners.
137.ch: Kansas City bands and the Blue Devils
137.q: People like Susan Strasberger, they thought that was the greatest thing they ever heard. Oh, you should have heard that rhythm section.

70.t: Basie's natural feel for tempo and people; Freddie Green
70.s: Hinton and Jackson say Basie set perfect dance tempos by natural feeling for the audience, with Freddie Green as Mr. Metronome.
70.q: You can't because this is such a natural thing there's no explanation to it. The man had such a natural feeling to play dance music and for swing and for tempo. He had such a natural feeling for tempo there's nothing that you can say about it because it's just a natural thing with him, which a…

73.t: Basie's secret: he wants to be sent
73.s: The Danses and Greene reflect on Basie's gift as rhythmic and on how simple his leadership is.
73.ch: Inside the Basie rhythm section and band family
73.q: That's right. It really is. You had to figure out that -- you could feel it. You could feel how Basie feels. You look at him -- I can -- and I'm sure everybody, you know, knows him after he's been there long enough to realize what's going on.
